I had to write custom subscribers to catch successful payment events and update the loyalty point database records accordingly.

It taught me that headless commerce gives you ultimate control over your user experience, but you pay for it in raw development hours. Now we can trigger highly specific reward triggers without paying monthly app store taxes to third-party platforms.

I spent four hours debugging a Razorpay integration only to find a missing slash.

We were testing the checkout flow for STRAYED last month and payments kept hanging in the pending state. The merchant dashboard showed successful charges, but our backend database refused to update the user orders.

It turned out our webhook listener was returning a 301 redirect instead of a clean 200 OK status. Razorpay was sending the payload, our server redirected the traffic because of an extra trailing slash in the URL configuration, and the webhook retries timed out.

Webhooks are silent killers when they fail because everything looks fine on the frontend. Now I always set up local tunneling with ngrok and mock payloads before touching production servers.

Our homepage load time was over five seconds because of unoptimized product images.

At Prettiva & Co., we had beautiful, high-res photos that our designer uploaded directly to the media library. But visitors on mobile connections in Bangalore were staring at blank white boxes for far too long.

I spent an afternoon changing our pipeline to convert all assets to next-gen WebP format and implemented lazy loading. We also sliced our JavaScript bundle size by lazy loading heavy non-critical components on the home page.

The load time dropped to under two seconds, and we saw an immediate drop in bounce rates. Good design is useless if the user leaves before the page actually renders on their phone screen.

Reducing friction is the cheapest way to increase conversion rates. You do not need fancy animations or complex loyalty popups, you just need to get out of the customer's way.

When we started STRAYED, we tried to follow a strict Gitflow model with develop, staging, release, and feature branches. We spent more time resolving complex merge conflicts and waiting for approvals than actually shipping code.

You have to match your development processes to the actual scale of your team. Keeping our git tree simple lets us ship hotfixes to our MedusaJS server in minutes rather than hours.

Our server response time spiked to three seconds during a small traffic surge last week.

We host our staging environment for Prettiva & Co. on a shared server instance. Everything worked fine with ten test users, but when we simulated a larger load, the CPU utilization shot straight to 100 percent.

The culprit was an unindexed query matching customer records against transaction histories during checkout. The database was performing a full table scan on every single load request, dragging down the whole server.

Adding a simple composite index on those foreign keys dropped the query time from 800ms to less than 10ms. It is a classic reminder that you do not need more expensive cloud instances, you just need efficient queries.

Designing websites in a high-speed office is very different from using them on the street.

When I test our web stores on my laptop over high-speed home fiber, everything loads in a blink. But the moment I try to load Prettiva & Co. while sitting in a Bangalore traffic jam with fluctuating 4G signals, the reality hits.

Heavy custom fonts and unoptimized tracker scripts cause massive layout shifts that make mobile buttons impossible to click. I had to audit our third-party script integrations and defer anything that was not critical for the initial paint.

We switched to system fonts for mobile views and implemented lightweight skeletons for lazy-loaded assets. Building for the worst-case network environment ensures your product actually works when your users need it most.
